text: A young poet is booked into a Washington, D.C. jail on a marijuana charge, and the cell becomes the room where he finds out what his voice is for. Marc Levin shoots Raymond Joshua's confinement as a place with its own politics: a gang leader on one side, a writing teacher on the other, and the arithmetic of who survives the judicial system running underneath. What holds the film together is spoken language under pressure, verse used less as art than as leverage. The 1998 Sundance jury gave it the U.S. Dramatic Grand Prize, which for a 104-minute film built around performance rather than incident is a wager on delivery over plot. It works because the poems are not decoration; they are the only tool Raymond has that the building cannot take from him.

Saga comes home to find his father has married the woman promised to him. Idrissa Ouedraogo builds Tilaï out of that single reversal and gives it 81 minutes, which is barely room to breathe and exactly enough to make the trap airtight. The two lovers resume, and by the village's reckoning what they are doing now has a different name and a different penalty. Everything is arranged in the open: Fulfulde spoken plainly, distances measured by walking, judgment handed down by people who have to keep living beside each other afterward. The Cannes jury gave it a Grand Prix in 1990. Burkina Faso in that decade produced work that treated custom not as scenery but as an argument with consequences, and this is one of the tightest cases of it.

Loretta Lynn wrote songs about her own life and sang them to people who recognized it, and the film takes that literally. Michael Apted follows the country singer out of poverty and into fame across 125 minutes, giving the early stretch enough time that the poverty registers as conditions rather than backstory. The performance carried Best Actress, and the film also took cinematography and editing, which for a music biography means the concert footage and the hollows were treated with the same care. It landed on the National Board of Review's top ten and later in the National Film Registry. What it declines to do is treat the ascent as inevitable; the career is a sequence of specific rooms, specific bookings, and a marriage that has to absorb every one of them.

Sixteen, pregnant, abandoned, and sharing a flat with a young gay man who has nowhere else either. Jo's arrangement with Geoffrey is the center of Tony Richardson's film, and it is offered without apology or explanation, which in Britain in 1961 was the whole provocation. Her mother is out chasing a new husband; the support that arrives instead comes from the person the era had least use for. Richardson keeps the northern streets and rented rooms visible enough that the money is always part of the conversation. The National Board of Review put it in its top ten that year, and it sits on the BFI's hundred British films. A hundred minutes, and the tenderness in it is entirely practical: two people covering for each other because no one else will.

A doctor trained in Germany comes back to Ethiopia and finds the junta has other uses for scientists. Haile Gerima gives Anberber 140 minutes to discover that neither his profession nor his childhood countryside offers shelter under the Mengistu regime, and the film moves through memory as freely as through the present, so that youth and ruin keep occupying the same frame. What is at stake is not survival but whether a person can still assemble a working life from what remains after his country's social fabric has been taken apart. Venice gave it a Grand Jury Prize. Amharic-language, made from inside a history most of its likely audience knows only as a headline, it treats displacement as something that happens to a man standing in his own village.

Brutus is persuaded, the knives come out, and then Mark Antony opens his mouth. Joseph L. Mankiewicz stages Shakespeare's political thriller in black and white on studio Rome, and the choice pays: the Academy handed it cinematography and art direction, awards that in 1953 usually went to color. Stripped of spectacle, the film becomes what the play always was, an argument about persuasion conducted by men who each believe they are the reasonable one. The conspirators calculate carefully and get the arithmetic of public feeling badly wrong. Best Actor came out of it, and the National Board of Review named it the year's best film. Two hours of speech as an instrument of force, filmed by a director who understood that talk is the most dangerous thing in the room.

Upstairs there is a shooting party; downstairs there is a staff that knows every guest's finances. Robert Altman takes the English country-house murder, a form built on the detective's clarity, and hands it to a filmmaker whose instinct is to let a dozen conversations run at once. The 1930s setting means the servants outnumber the suspects, and the film keeps drifting below stairs where the real information lives. It won Best Picture, Best Director, and costume design, and the ensemble took the SAG award, which is the right prize for a film with no lead. What Altman is actually filming is a labor arrangement: who serves whom, who overhears what, and how a household that runs on invisibility responds when someone finally has to be seen.

Two liberal parents have raised their daughter on principles, and one afternoon she brings the principles home to dinner. Stanley Kramer sets almost everything in a single house across a single day, which is a stage playwright's structure applied to the year 1967, when the question of an interracial marriage was still being decided in courtrooms. The pressure is procedural rather than dramatic: an engagement announced, an evening to get through, and adults discovering what their stated beliefs cost when made specific. The Academy gave it Best Actress and Best Original Screenplay; it later entered the National Film Registry. The film's honesty is in showing that agreement in the abstract and consent at the table are separate acts, and that the second one is harder.

An actor gets one last shot at the part that could restore him, and he is drinking. George Seaton builds the film around that offer and around the wife who has been managing the wreckage long enough that everyone else reads her as the problem. The theater setting gives it a hard deadline: rehearsals, previews, a producer's patience running out, and a man who has to be sober by a date on a calendar. Best Actor and Best Actress both came from it, which is the correct verdict on a picture that is essentially two performances circling a third party's mistaken assumption. At 104 minutes it stays inside the domestic argument rather than the comeback, and the argument is about who has been telling the truth about whom.

A man with a thriving dealership and a beautiful wife falls for the plain temp in his office. Bertrand Blier takes the premise everyone would call implausible and refuses to explain it away, which is the film's whole comic nerve: desire that declines to follow the logic of appearances, and a marriage that cannot absorb the insult of being left for someone less. Ninety-one minutes, French, and the tone keeps sliding — farce, then something colder, then back. Cannes gave it a Grand Prix in 1989 and the Césars named it best film with a best actress prize. Blier is not interested in whether the affair is justified. He is interested in what it does to a woman told, in effect, that her advantages were never the point.

Four Montreal academics cook dinner and talk about sex; across town, four women work out and talk about the same thing. Denys Arcand keeps the two groups apart for most of the film so their accounts can be compared before they are reconciled, and then puts everyone at one table. The talk is the event. These are people trained to theorize their own appetites, and the comedy comes from how fluently they narrate conduct they have no intention of changing. In French, 101 minutes, made in Quebec in 1986 and sent to the Academy, where it took Best International Feature. Under the banter is a colder proposition about a society that has turned its attention inward, and the film lets the guests supply the evidence themselves.

The FBI agent is the least stable person in the room, and he is the one holding the leash. David O. Russell puts a conman and his partner to work for the bureau and then lets the operation swell past anyone's ability to control it, out into New Jersey politics and toward the Mafia, at which point the question stops being whether the sting succeeds and becomes who is running whom. The performances took Best Actor and Best Actress; costume design won too, and it matters, because everyone here is dressed as the person they are pretending to be. The New York Film Critics Circle named it the year's best film and the ensemble took the SAG award. Everyone is improvising, and confidence is the only currency in circulation.
